newsitem.title: USA: Lloyd-Webber loses counterclaim plagiarism case.
newsitem.headline: Lloyd-Webber loses counterclaim plagiarism case.

text.p: A New York federal judge ruled on Wednesday that British composer Andrew Lloyd Webber failed to establish a counterclaim in a music plagiarism case.

In a 26-page opinion, U.S. District Judge Shirley Wohl Kram found that Lloyd Webber had not established that Ray Repp, the folk music composer who wrote the religious song, "Till You", copied Lloyd Webber's "Close Every Door" from the musical "Joseph and the Amazing Technicolor Dreamcoat."
"Although the songs share some musical devices, such as rising arpeggios and descending tetra chords, such tools are among the most common devices used in music," the judge said.
"The fact that the songs share use of a 'door metaphor' does not support an inference of copying in the present case," the judge concluded.

At a non-jury trial held in Manhattan federal court in September, Repp testified that he used similar "door" imagery in at least three other works ... prior to the first performance of "Close Every Door" in 1969.
Repp wrote "Till You" in 1976 and had the work copyrighted in 1978.

"The court's finding that Repp did not have access to Lloyd Webber's 1969 composition 'Close Every Door' is surprising in view of the success and general worldwide awareness of 'Joseph and The Amazing Technicolor Dreamcoat,' Peter Brown, a spokesman for Lloyd Webber said.
The British composer is considering whether to appeal Wednesday's decision, he said.

The legal battle began in 1990 after Repp heard the main theme from "Phantom" which he said sounded like "Till You". Meanwhile lawyers for Lloyd Webber filed a counterclaim, alleging that "Till You" copied notes and melodies from "Joseph and the Amazing Technicolor Dreamcoat."
Lawyers for Repp said they would now proceed with their main claim against Lloyd Webber, in which Repp alleges that when Lloyd Webber wrote "Phantom of the Opera", he copied Repp's song "Till You".

"The opinion today permits us to go forward with our main claim, which we were unable to do until the counterclaim was resolved," William Coulson, the Chicago-based attorney for Repp said. "The monetary damages will be based on Lloyd Webber's profits from 'Phantom.' We will be seeking tens of millions of dollars," the lawyer said.
Lloyd Webber's other major works include "Jesus Christ Superstar," "Cats", "Evita" and "Sunset Boulevard."
